overview: Executor memory tuning is the practice of correctly sizing the JVM heap, off-heap region, and container overhead of Spark executors so that tasks have enough working memory for execution and caching without triggering OutOfMemoryError or having the resource manager kill the container.

Spark uses a Unified Memory Manager where the configured spark.executor.memory heap is carved into a fixed 300MB reserved region, a user memory region for your data structures and UDFs, and a unified region (spark.memory.fraction, default 0.6) shared elastically between execution (shuffles, joins, aggregations, sorts) and storage (cached blocks).

Debugging OOM means distinguishing three distinct failure modes — a JVM heap OOM (java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space), a container killed by the resource manager for exceeding its total memory (heap + overhead), and a GC overhead limit exceeded error — because each points to a different knob (heap, memoryOverhead, or partitioning/skew).
learningObjectives: Understand the full executor memory model: reserved 300MB, user memory, the unified execution/storage region governed by spark.memory.fraction and spark.memory.storageFraction, off-heap memory, and memoryOverhead.
Learn to read the three canonical OOM signatures (Java heap space, YARN/K8s container killed, GC overhead limit exceeded) and map each to its root cause and correct fix.
Master the diagnostic workflow using the Spark UI Executors tab, GC logs, heap dumps, and spill metrics, and the concrete configs (spark-submit --conf) to resolve OOM in production PySpark jobs.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Executor memory tuning is the configuration of a Spark executor's memory budget across two dimensions: the JVM on-heap size (spark.executor.memory) partitioned by the Unified Memory Manager into a 300MB reserved region, a user region (1 - spark.memory.fraction of usable heap), and a unified region (spark.memory.fraction of usable heap) dynamically split between execution and storage with a soft boundary anchored by spark.memory.storageFraction; and the container total, which is on-heap plus off-heap (spark.memory.offHeap.size) plus spark.executor.memoryOverhead (default max(384MB, 0.1 * executor memory)) covering JVM internals, Netty network buffers, and the PySpark python worker. OOM debugging is the process of identifying whether a failure originates in the JVM heap, in the total container footprint policed by the resource manager, or in excessive garbage collection, and applying the corresponding remediation.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of each executor as a worker with a backpack of a fixed size. Part of the backpack is permanently reserved for the worker's own tools (reserved + user memory). The rest is a shared pouch that flexes between two jobs: doing the current task (execution) and holding cached snacks for later (storage). If the worker tries to stuff in more than the backpack holds, the backpack rips — that is a Java heap OOM. But the worker also carries extra gear strapped outside the backpack (overhead + python process); if the total load exceeds what the building allows, security throws the worker out entirely — that is the container being killed. Tuning is deciding how big the backpack is, how much flex the shared pouch gets, and how much room to leave for the outside gear.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Before Spark 1.6 (2016), executors used a static memory manager that hard-split the heap into fixed fractions for execution (spark.shuffle.memoryFraction) and storage (spark.storage.memoryFraction). This rigidity meant a shuffle-heavy job could OOM even while a large cache region sat mostly empty. Spark 1.6 introduced the Unified Memory Manager (SPARK-10000), which merged the two into one elastic region where execution can borrow from storage and evict cached blocks when it needs room, drastically reducing avoidable OOMs. Later releases added off-heap execution/storage via Tungsten (spark.memory.offHeap) to escape JVM GC pressure, and refined memoryOverhead handling for the PySpark python worker (spark.executor.pyspark.memory) so that Python-side memory could be bounded and accounted for separately.

whyItMatters.business: OOM failures cause nightly pipelines to miss SLAs, delay business-critical dashboards, and force expensive on-call reruns; correctly tuned executors turn a flaky job into a predictable one, protecting downstream reports and revenue-impacting decisions.
whyItMatters.engineering: Distinguishing a heap OOM from a container kill saves hours of blind config-flailing; the right diagnosis (increase overhead vs. increase partitions vs. fix skew) is the difference between a five-minute fix and a week of trial and error.
whyItMatters.scalability: Memory tuning determines how large a dataset a fixed cluster can process; right-sizing executors and partitions lets the same cluster handle 10x the data without adding nodes, and lets jobs scale horizontally by keeping per-partition working sets bounded.
whyItMatters.cost: Over-provisioning memory to mask OOM wastes cloud spend on idle RAM, while under-provisioning causes retries that burn compute; tuning to the actual working set minimizes both wasted memory and retry cost on pay-per-hour clusters.
whyItMatters.reliability: Container kills and heap OOMs trigger task and stage retries that can cascade into whole-job failure; a properly sized memory budget with headroom for skew and overhead is the primary lever for job reliability under varying data volumes.

coreComponents.name: Reserved Memory (300MB)
coreComponents.definition: A fixed 300MB slice of every executor's heap that Spark sets aside before any of its own memory accounting begins.
coreComponents.purpose: To guarantee a safety buffer for internal Spark objects and to prevent the executor from being starved when heap is very small.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Held out of both user and unified regions; the usable heap for Spark's memory manager is (spark.executor.memory - 300MB).
coreComponents.examples: With spark.executor.memory=4g, usable memory = 4096MB - 300MB = 3796MB before the fraction split is applied.

coreComponents.name: User Memory
coreComponents.definition: The portion of usable heap not managed by the unified region, computed as (1 - spark.memory.fraction) of usable memory (default 0.4).
coreComponents.purpose: To hold user data structures created in transformations, UDF working memory, and internal metadata Spark does not track in the unified pool.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Stores objects your code allocates (large collections in a mapPartitions, hashmaps in UDFs) and Spark internal metadata not counted against execution/storage.
coreComponents.examples: With 3796MB usable and spark.memory.fraction=0.6, user memory ≈ 0.4 * 3796 ≈ 1518MB.

coreComponents.name: Unified Region (Execution + Storage)
coreComponents.definition: The spark.memory.fraction (default 0.6) share of usable heap, elastically split between execution and storage with a soft boundary at spark.memory.storageFraction (default 0.5).
coreComponents.purpose: To let shuffles/joins/aggregations (execution) and cached blocks (storage) share one pool, borrowing from each other on demand to minimize OOM.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Execution memory for sorts, hash tables, and shuffle buffers can evict cached storage blocks when needed; storage can occupy free execution space but is evicted first under pressure.
coreComponents.examples: With 3796MB usable, unified ≈ 0.6 * 3796 ≈ 2277MB; storage floor ≈ 0.5 * 2277 ≈ 1138MB, the rest borrowable by execution.

coreComponents.name: Off-Heap Memory
coreComponents.definition: Memory allocated outside the JVM heap via spark.memory.offHeap.enabled and spark.memory.offHeap.size, used by Tungsten for execution and storage.
coreComponents.purpose: To hold serialized/binary data in native memory, avoiding JVM garbage collection overhead and reducing GC pauses on large working sets.
coreComponents.responsibilities: When enabled, execution and storage can additionally use the off-heap pool; this memory is not part of the heap but counts toward the container's total footprint.
coreComponents.examples: spark.memory.offHeap.enabled=true with spark.memory.offHeap.size=2g adds 2GB of GC-free execution/storage capacity.

coreComponents.name: Memory Overhead (spark.executor.memoryOverhead)
coreComponents.definition: Non-heap memory reserved in the container for JVM internals, thread stacks, Netty buffers, and native libraries; default max(384MB, 0.1 * spark.executor.memory).
coreComponents.purpose: To account for memory Spark uses outside the managed heap so the resource manager container is sized to include it and does not get killed.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Covers off-heap shuffle/network (Netty) buffers, JVM metaspace and code cache, and — historically — the PySpark python worker unless spark.executor.pyspark.memory is set.
coreComponents.examples: For spark.executor.memory=8g, default overhead = max(384MB, 819MB) = 819MB; total container request ≈ 8g + ~819MB.

coreComponents.name: PySpark Python Worker Memory (spark.executor.pyspark.memory)
coreComponents.definition: An optional cap on the memory used by the python worker processes that run PySpark UDFs and RDD python code, separate from the JVM heap.
coreComponents.purpose: To bound and account for python-side memory (pandas UDFs, python data structures) that lives in a separate process from the JVM.
coreComponents.responsibilities: When set, limits python worker RSS; python memory otherwise draws from memoryOverhead / container headroom and is a common hidden cause of container kills in PySpark.
coreComponents.examples: spark.executor.pyspark.memory=2g caps each python worker so a memory-hungry pandas UDF cannot silently blow the container budget.

internalWorking: At executor startup, Spark computes usable memory = spark.executor.memory - 300MB reserved; it then splits usable memory into user memory = (1 - spark.memory.fraction) * usable and the unified region = spark.memory.fraction * usable.

Within the unified region, execution and storage share one pool: execution memory (for sort buffers, aggregation hash maps, shuffle spill buffers, join hash tables) can grow and, if needed, evict cached storage blocks down to the spark.memory.storageFraction floor; storage can expand into unused execution space but is the first to be reclaimed under pressure.

When execution memory is exhausted even after evicting evictable storage, the operator (sort, aggregate, shuffle) spills to disk rather than immediately failing; spill bytes and spill records are recorded and shown in the Spark UI as a signal of memory pressure.

If a single task's live objects still cannot fit — for example a huge broadcast, an oversized single partition, or a collect() pulling too much to one task — the JVM throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space, or if the JVM spends most of its time in GC reclaiming almost nothing it throws GC overhead limit exceeded.

Independently, the resource manager (YARN NodeManager or Kubernetes) monitors the container's total physical memory = JVM heap + off-heap + memoryOverhead + python worker; if the aggregate exceeds the container limit it kills the container with a 'Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits ... consider boosting spark.executor.memoryOverhead' message, which is distinct from an in-JVM heap OOM.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: spark.executor.memory (JVM heap) -> subtract 300MB Reserved -> Usable Memory -> split by spark.memory.fraction into User Memory (0.4) and Unified Region (0.6) -> Unified Region elastically split by spark.memory.storageFraction into Execution and Storage -> spill to disk under pressure -> if heap exhausted: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError -> separately: Heap + Off-Heap (offHeap.size) + memoryOverhead + pyspark.memory = Container Total -> resource manager kills container if Container Total > limit
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. spark-submit requests executors of spark.executor.memory=8g with default overhead max(384MB, 0.8g)=819MB, so each YARN container is sized ~8.8GB.
2. Inside the 8g heap, Spark reserves 300MB, leaving ~7892MB usable; user memory ≈ 0.4*7892 ≈ 3157MB, unified region ≈ 0.6*7892 ≈ 4735MB.

3. A groupBy aggregation builds hash maps in execution memory; as it grows it evicts cached blocks down to the storage floor (~0.5*4735 ≈ 2368MB) and, when still short, spills partial aggregates to disk (visible as spill in the UI).

4. A skewed key funnels a huge partition to one task; its hash table exceeds available execution memory and cannot spill fast enough, so the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space on that executor.

5. Alternatively, a pandas UDF spawns python workers whose RSS plus the JVM heap exceeds the 8.8GB container; the NodeManager kills the container with 'Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits', which is fixed by raising memoryOverhead or capping spark.executor.pyspark.memory, not by raising heap.

keyTerminology.meaning: Fraction of usable heap (post-reserved) given to the unified execution+storage region; default 0.6.
keyTerminology.importance: Raising it gives more room for shuffles and cache but shrinks user memory for your own objects; the central lever for execution-heavy vs. UDF-heavy jobs.

keyTerminology.meaning: The soft floor (default 0.5) of the unified region reserved for storage that execution cannot evict below.
keyTerminology.importance: Protects cached data from being fully evicted by execution; lower it for shuffle-heavy jobs, raise it for cache-heavy iterative jobs.

keyTerminology.meaning: Non-heap container memory (default max(384MB, 0.1*executor memory)) for JVM internals, Netty, and python.
keyTerminology.importance: The single most common fix for 'Container killed by YARN' errors; too small causes container kills even when the heap is fine.

keyTerminology.meaning: A JVM error thrown when more than 98% of time is spent in GC recovering less than 2% of the heap.
keyTerminology.importance: Signals the heap is nearly full and thrashing; indicates you need more heap, fewer concurrent tasks per JVM, or off-heap memory rather than a simple retry.

keyTerminology.meaning: Writing execution data (sort/aggregate/shuffle buffers) to local disk when execution memory is exhausted.
keyTerminology.importance: Spill is a graceful degradation that prevents OOM; heavy spill in the UI is the early warning that a job is memory-starved before it actually fails.

importantConcepts.concept: Heap OOM vs. Container Kill vs. GC Overhead
importantConcepts.explanation: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space means a task could not fit its live objects in the JVM heap (fix: bigger heap, more partitions, avoid huge collect/broadcast, fix skew). 'Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits' means the total physical footprint (heap + off-heap + overhead + python) exceeded the container (fix: raise spark.executor.memoryOverhead, cap pyspark.memory). GC overhead limit exceeded means the JVM is thrashing on GC (fix: more heap, fewer cores per executor, off-heap). Diagnosing which one you have is the first and most important step.

importantConcepts.concept: Cores per Executor and Concurrent Task Memory
importantConcepts.explanation: Each executor runs spark.executor.cores tasks concurrently, and they all share the same heap; execution memory is divided among them. Fewer cores per executor means each task gets a larger share of memory (fewer OOMs) at the cost of some parallelism, which is why reducing spark.executor.cores from 5 to 3 is a classic OOM fix when tasks are memory-heavy.

importantConcepts.concept: Partition Size as the Root Lever
importantConcepts.explanation: OOM is usually a per-partition problem: a task's working set is roughly proportional to its input/shuffle partition size. Increasing spark.sql.shuffle.partitions or repartitioning shrinks each partition so the per-task working set fits, which is often a cleaner fix than throwing more heap at the problem. Aim for partitions in the ~100-200MB range.

variationsAndTypes: **On-heap tuning:** Adjusting spark.executor.memory, spark.memory.fraction, and spark.memory.storageFraction to size the managed JVM pools.
**Off-heap tuning:** Enabling spark.memory.offHeap.enabled with spark.memory.offHeap.size to move execution/storage to GC-free native memory for large working sets.
**Overhead tuning:** Raising spark.executor.memoryOverhead (or spark.executor.memoryOverheadFactor in Spark 3.3+) to satisfy container limits for Netty/JVM/native usage.
**PySpark-specific tuning:** Setting spark.executor.pyspark.memory to bound python worker RSS for UDF/pandas-heavy jobs.
**Parallelism-based tuning:** Reducing spark.executor.cores or increasing partitions so each concurrent task's memory share is larger, avoiding OOM without adding RAM.

**Kubernetes vs YARN:** On K8s the pod memory limit (heap + overhead + off-heap) is enforced by cgroups (OOMKilled, exit 137); on YARN the NodeManager enforces it with the 'Container killed' message — same concept, different symptom text.
advantages: **Predictable, SLA-friendly jobs:** Correctly sized memory eliminates random OOM failures and retries, making runtimes stable across data volumes.
**Efficient resource use:** Right-sizing avoids over-provisioning RAM, lowering cluster cost while still fitting the working set.
**Graceful degradation via spill:** The unified manager spills to disk under pressure instead of failing outright, buying resilience.
**Elastic execution/storage sharing:** The unified region lets a shuffle-heavy or cache-heavy job reuse the same pool without static tuning.
**Off-heap escape valve:** Off-heap memory sidesteps GC pauses for very large working sets that would otherwise thrash the heap.
disadvantages: **Diagnosis complexity:** Three different OOM signatures require different fixes; misreading them leads to wasted configuration changes.
**Overhead is easy to forget:** The container total (heap + overhead + python) is larger than spark.executor.memory, and forgetting overhead causes surprise container kills.
**Skew defeats uniform tuning:** A single hot key can OOM one task no matter how well the average is sized, requiring skew-specific fixes.
**Spill has a performance cost:** Avoiding OOM via disk spill trades memory pressure for I/O, which can dominate runtime if severe.
**Python memory is opaque:** PySpark python worker memory lives outside the JVM and is hard to observe, often surfacing only as container kills.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Tune executor memory whenever you see OOM/container-kill errors, heavy spill, high GC time in the Executors tab, or when scaling a job to larger data; start by increasing partitions and overhead before blindly increasing heap.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Do not simply keep raising spark.executor.memory as a first reflex — an oversized heap causes long GC pauses and wastes RAM. Avoid huge single executors (fat JVMs) when many small tasks would parallelize better; for skew-driven OOM, fix the skew rather than tuning memory.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: An executor is like a food truck. The truck's total weight limit set by the road authority is the container limit (heap + overhead + python); exceed it and the truck gets pulled over and impounded — that's a container kill. Inside, the kitchen counter is the JVM heap: a fixed reserved corner for the register (300MB reserved), a section for the chef's personal tools (user memory), and a flexible prep area shared between cooking the current order (execution) and storing prepped ingredients for later (storage). If an order is so big it can't fit on the counter even after clearing prepped ingredients, the counter overflows — a heap OOM. If the chef spends all shift frantically cleaning to make room and barely cooks, that's GC overhead limit exceeded.

commonMisconceptions.reality: If the failure is 'Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits', the fix is usually more memoryOverhead or capped python memory; and a bigger heap can worsen GC pauses. The right fix depends on which OOM signature you have.

commonMisconceptions.myth: spark.executor.memory is the total memory the executor uses.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The container also holds memoryOverhead (JVM internals, Netty), off-heap memory, and the PySpark python worker; the true container footprint is heap + off-heap + overhead + python, which is why containers get killed even when the heap looks fine.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Storage (cache) and execution memory are separate fixed pools.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Since Spark 1.6 they share one unified region; execution can evict cached blocks down to the storageFraction floor, so caching too aggressively can starve execution and vice versa.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Scale by keeping per-partition working set bounded (~100-200MB): increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions or repartition as data grows so per-task memory stays constant even as total volume rises, rather than continually growing executor heaps.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Leave headroom in memoryOverhead and heap for data-volume variability and skew; jobs sized exactly to today's data OOM when tomorrow's data grows 20%. Configure task/stage retries but treat repeated OOM retries as a tuning signal, not a solution.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: OOM kills tasks and can lose executors; enable the external shuffle service so shuffle files survive executor loss, and ensure stage retries can recover. Heap dumps on OOM (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError) preserve evidence for post-mortem without blocking recovery.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch the Executors tab for GC Time (should be a small fraction of task time), Storage Memory usage, and failed tasks; watch the Stages tab for spill (memory and disk). Export executor JVM metrics (heap used, GC) to Prometheus/Grafana for trend alerts.
productionConsiderations.security: Heap dumps written on OOM can contain sensitive data in memory; write them to a secured directory, restrict access, and scrub or delete them promptly. Encrypt spilled shuffle data (spark.io.encryption.enabled) since it lands on local disk under memory pressure.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Right-size rather than over-provision: profile the actual working set and set heap/overhead just above it with a safety margin. Prefer more, smaller executors with fewer cores over fat JVMs when it reduces GC and OOM, and use off-heap only when GC is the proven bottleneck.
productionConsiderations.performance: Minimize GC by avoiding oversized heaps, reducing per-executor cores when tasks are memory-heavy, using off-heap for large binary working sets, and eliminating spill by right-sizing partitions; keep GC time under ~10% of task time as a target.

codeExamples.title: Computing the Executor Memory Budget and Setting Configs via spark-submit
codeExamples.overview: Shows the exact memory-model arithmetic for a chosen executor size and the spark-submit configuration that requests the corresponding container, including overhead.
codeExamples.code:
# spark-submit with an explicit, correctly-sized memory budget
spark-submit \
  --master yarn \
  --deploy-mode cluster \
  --num-executors 20 \
  --executor-cores 4 \
  --executor-memory 8g \
  --conf spark.executor.memoryOverhead=1536m \
  --conf spark.memory.fraction=0.6 \
  --conf spark.memory.storageFraction=0.5 \
  --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=800 \
  --conf spark.executor.pyspark.memory=2g \
  job.py

# Memory arithmetic for --executor-memory 8g (8192 MB heap):
#   Reserved            = 300 MB
#   Usable              = 8192 - 300            = 7892 MB
#   User memory         = (1 - 0.6) * 7892      = 3157 MB
#   Unified region      = 0.6 * 7892            = 4735 MB
#     Storage floor     = 0.5 * 4735            = 2368 MB (execution cannot evict below this)
#     Execution (max)   = up to 4735 MB when storage is empty
#   Container total     = 8192 heap + 1536 overhead (+ up to 2g python) ~= 9.7-11.7 GB
codeExamples.breakdown: --executor-memory sets the JVM heap; Spark subtracts 300MB reserved, then splits by spark.memory.fraction (0.6) into user (0.4) and unified (0.6), and the unified region is soft-split at spark.memory.storageFraction (0.5). --conf spark.executor.memoryOverhead reserves non-heap container space for Netty/JVM/python so the container is not killed; spark.executor.pyspark.memory caps python worker RSS. The container the resource manager allocates is heap + overhead (+ off-heap + python), which is why it is larger than 8g.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Executor container requested ~= 8192MB heap + 1536MB overhead = 9728MB (plus python budget). In the Spark UI Executors tab each executor shows ~4.7GB Storage Memory capacity and task memory drawn from the unified region; GC Time stays a small fraction of task time when correctly sized.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting overhead: setting --executor-memory close to the node RAM leaves no room for the ~10-20% overhead, so YARN kills the container. Setting spark.memory.fraction too high starves user memory used by UDFs and large driver-side collections.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Size partitions so each task's input is ~100-200MB (here 800 shuffle partitions for a large dataset), and start overhead at ~15-20% of heap for PySpark jobs since the python worker draws from container headroom.

codeExamples.title: Reproducing and Diagnosing a Java Heap OOM from a Huge collect()
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates the classic driver/executor heap OOM caused by pulling too much data to memory, and the correct incremental alternative.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("OOMDemo").getOrCreate()

df = spark.read.parquet("/data/events.parquet")  # 500M rows

# ANTI-PATTERN: pulls all 500M rows into driver JVM heap -> OOM
# rows = df.collect()               # java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
# big = df.groupBy("user_id").agg({"*": "count"}).collect()  # also risky if many keys

# CORRECT: never materialize the whole dataset in one JVM.
# 1) Aggregate/filter down first, then collect only a small result
small = (df.filter(col("is_active"))
           .groupBy("country")
           .count())          # tiny result, safe to collect
result = small.collect()

# 2) If you must process every row, write out or use toLocalIterator (streams partitions)
for row in df.select("user_id").toLocalIterator():
    pass  # processes one partition at a time, bounded memory

# 3) For large outputs, write to storage instead of collecting
df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/output/events_processed")
codeExamples.breakdown: df.collect() serializes every partition back to the driver JVM and holds them all in heap at once, causing java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space on large data. The fix is to reduce before collecting (filter/aggregate to a small result), use toLocalIterator() which streams one partition at a time with bounded memory, or write results to storage. The same OOM appears on executors when a single task materializes too much (e.g., a giant broadcast or an exploded join).
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Without the fix: driver log shows 'java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space' and the job aborts. With the fix: small.collect() returns a handful of rows, toLocalIterator streams safely, and the write completes; the Executors tab shows no failed tasks and low GC time.
codeExamples.commonIssues: collect() and toPandas() on large frames are the number-one cause of driver heap OOM. Broadcasting a table larger than spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (or an explicit broadcast() of a big table) causes executor heap OOM.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Always filter/aggregate before collect; prefer write() or toLocalIterator() for large data; raise spark.driver.memory for legitimately large-but-bounded results; keep broadcast tables well under a few hundred MB.

codeExamples.title: Enabling GC Logging and Heap Dumps to Debug OOM, Plus Off-Heap
codeExamples.overview: Configures JVM diagnostics (GC details, heap dump on OOM) and off-heap memory so you can root-cause and remediate memory failures.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = (SparkSession.builder
    .appName("MemoryDebug")
    # --- Diagnostics: print GC details and dump heap on OOM ---
    .config("spark.executor.extraJavaOptions",
            "-XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+PrintGCTimeStamps "
            "-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError "
            "-XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/log/spark/heapdumps "
            "-XX:+UseG1GC")
    # --- Off-heap: move execution/storage to GC-free native memory ---
    .config("spark.memory.offHeap.enabled", "true")
    .config("spark.memory.offHeap.size", "3g")
    # --- Reduce concurrent tasks per JVM so each gets more memory ---
    .config("spark.executor.cores", "3")
    # --- Bump overhead for PySpark / Netty / native ---
    .config("spark.executor.memoryOverhead", "2g")
    .getOrCreate())

# Read spill metrics after a shuffle-heavy stage to confirm memory pressure
df = spark.read.parquet("/data/big.parquet")
agg = df.groupBy("key").sum("value")
agg.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/output/agg")
# In the Spark UI Stages tab, inspect 'Spill (Memory)' and 'Spill (Disk)' columns;
# non-zero spill => the stage is memory-starved (increase partitions / heap / off-heap).
codeExamples.breakdown: spark.executor.extraJavaOptions passes JVM flags: -XX:+PrintGCDetails logs GC pauses (read in stderr / executor logs to spot GC overhead), -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError writes an .hprof file on OOM for analysis in Eclipse MAT, and -XX:+UseG1GC uses a pause-friendly collector. Off-heap (offHeap.enabled/size) adds GC-free execution/storage capacity. Lowering spark.executor.cores gives each concurrent task a larger memory share. Raising memoryOverhead prevents container kills. Spill columns in the UI confirm whether the stage is memory-starved.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Executor stderr shows GC pause lines (e.g., '[GC pause (G1 Evacuation Pause) ... 512M->200M(4096M), 0.03s]'); on OOM a heap dump appears at /var/log/spark/heapdumps/*.hprof. The Stages tab shows Spill (Memory)/Spill (Disk) values that drop toward zero after enabling off-heap and increasing overhead.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Setting HeapDumpPath to a small or non-existent directory causes the dump to fail; large heap dumps can fill local disk. Off-heap size counts toward the container total, so you must also raise the container limit or you trade a heap OOM for a container kill.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use G1GC for large heaps to shorten pauses; keep off-heap size explicit and account for it in the container total; treat non-zero disk spill as the trigger to increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions before increasing heap.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A fintech data team runs a nightly PySpark job that enriches 2 billion card transactions with a merchant dimension and computes per-merchant daily aggregates. The job intermittently fails with 'Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits' and occasionally 'java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space', missing the 6am SLA and requiring manual reruns.
endToEndExample.inputData: transactions.parquet (2B rows: txn_id, card_id, merchant_id, amount, ts) at ~600GB, and merchants.parquet (5M rows: merchant_id, category, region) at ~400MB. Transaction volume is skewed: a few large merchants account for 15% of all rows.
endToEndExample.architecture: PySpark on YARN with 40 executors, initially 5 cores and 12g each with default overhead. DataFrame API compiled by Catalyst; a pandas UDF computes a risk score, spawning python workers per executor. External shuffle service enabled.
processingSteps: 1. Diagnose: read the Executors tab — GC Time is ~35% of task time on several executors and multiple tasks failed; the driver log shows both a container-kill message (pointing at overhead/python) and a heap-space OOM (pointing at skew/partition size).

2. Attribute the container kill: the pandas UDF's python workers plus the 12g heap exceed the container; raise spark.executor.memoryOverhead from default (~1.2g) to 3g and set spark.executor.pyspark.memory=3g to bound python.

3. Attribute the heap OOM: the skewed merchants create giant partitions in the groupBy; increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions from 200 to 2000 and enable AQE skew handling (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled + skewJoin) to split hot partitions.
4. Reduce GC/concurrency pressure: lower spark.executor.cores from 5 to 3 so each task gets a larger heap share, and switch to G1GC; broadcast the 400MB merchant dimension to avoid a shuffle join.
5. Re-run with GC logging and -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError enabled to confirm the fix and capture evidence if any OOM recurs; monitor spill columns in the Stages tab.
endToEndExample.output: A partitioned Parquet dataset of per-merchant daily aggregates plus a risk score, written to /output/merchant_daily. The Spark UI shows GC time dropped to ~8%, zero failed tasks, and disk spill near zero after right-sizing partitions.
endToEndExample.monitoring: The Executors tab confirms GC Time under 10% and Storage Memory well within capacity; the Stages tab shows Spill (Memory)/Spill (Disk) at zero for the aggregation stage; Prometheus alerts on executor heap-used > 85% and GC time > 15% were added.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If a container is still killed, YARN retries the task on another executor; the external shuffle service preserves shuffle files so the retry does not recompute the whole stage. Heap dumps written on any residual OOM are analyzed in Eclipse MAT to find the dominant object (confirming skew), and repeated OOM retries trigger an on-call alert rather than silent looping.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Separating the container-kill fix (overhead + pyspark.memory) from the heap-OOM fix (partitions + skew handling + fewer cores) eliminated both failure modes: the job went from ~30% nightly failure rate to zero over 60 nights, runtime dropped from ~2h10m (with retries) to 48 minutes, and cluster cost fell because right-sizing removed the need for oversized 24g fat executors.

industryUseCases.problem: Petabyte-scale ETL jobs on autoscaling clusters intermittently fail with container kills and heap OOMs as input volumes and data skew shift night to night.
industryUseCases.solution: Engineers standardize executor sizing (moderate heap, generous memoryOverhead for the Netty/python footprint), enforce partition targets near 128MB, and use AQE plus skew handling so hot partitions are split rather than OOMing a single task; GC logs and heap dumps feed automated diagnostics.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fewer OOM-driven retries cut cluster-hour cost, jobs meet SLAs reliably across variable data volumes, and standardized sizing reduces per-team tuning toil.

industryUseCases.problem: Large joins and aggregations over trip and payment data hit GC overhead limits and container kills when memory-heavy UDFs run alongside wide shuffles on the same JVMs.
industryUseCases.solution: Uber reduces cores per executor for memory-heavy stages, enables off-heap memory to escape GC pauses on large binary working sets, bounds python worker memory for pandas UDFs, and monitors spill/GC metrics to catch pressure before failure.
industryUseCases.benefits: Lower GC pause time improves throughput, container kills drop sharply, and off-heap usage keeps very large working sets stable without oversized heaps.

industryUseCases.problem: Customers run complex notebooks that call collect()/toPandas() on huge DataFrames and broadcast oversized tables, causing driver and executor heap OOMs.
industryUseCases.solution: The platform surfaces memory metrics and spill in the UI, warns on large broadcasts, provides AQE for runtime partition/skew re-optimization, and guidance to replace collect() with toLocalIterator()/write and to raise driver/overhead memory appropriately.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fewer user-triggered OOMs, clearer root-cause visibility, and adaptive re-optimization that removes much manual memory tuning.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Scale by bounding per-partition working set (~100-200MB) via spark.sql.shuffle.partitions and repartition, and by adding executors rather than growing heaps; AQE coalesce/skew features keep task memory uniform as data grows, so the same executor template handles 10x volume without re-tuning heap.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: OOM and container kills lose tasks and sometimes whole executors; the external shuffle service preserves shuffle files so stage retries recover without full recomputation, and configured task/stage max failures absorb transient memory spikes while heap dumps preserve evidence for post-mortem.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: The driver holds job state and is itself a memory risk (collect/toPandas OOM the driver); run in cluster mode with driver restart, size spark.driver.memory for legitimate results, and never materialize large datasets on the driver so a single memory spike cannot take down the application.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: For long or expensive pipelines, checkpoint intermediate results to reliable storage so an OOM-induced failure resumes from the last durable stage instead of the start; keep heap dumps and GC logs archived to reconstruct and prevent recurrence of memory incidents.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Keep GC time under ~10% of task time by avoiding oversized heaps, reducing cores per executor for memory-heavy tasks, using G1GC on large heaps, enabling off-heap for large binary working sets, broadcasting small tables to avoid shuffle memory, and eliminating spill by right-sizing partitions.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Right-size to the measured working set instead of over-provisioning; prefer many moderate executors over fat JVMs when it reduces GC/OOM, use off-heap only when GC is the proven bottleneck, and remove retry-driven waste by fixing the root memory cause rather than raising heap blindly.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Heap dumps and spilled shuffle data can contain sensitive records; write heap dumps to a locked-down path with restricted access and prompt deletion, and enable spark.io.encryption.enabled so on-disk spill (frequent under memory pressure) is encrypted at rest, with spark.network.crypto.enabled for shuffle transfer.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use the Executors tab (GC Time, Storage Memory, failed tasks), the Stages tab (Spill Memory/Disk, task duration distribution for skew), executor JVM metrics via the metrics system to Prometheus/Grafana, and GC logs; the History Server preserves this for post-mortem after OOM incidents.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Memory-driven task retries must be deterministic to remain correct; avoid non-deterministic UDFs so recomputed partitions after an OOM retry yield identical results, and validate aggregate row counts and totals against source to ensure no data was dropped by partial failures.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log and alert on OOM signatures (grep executor logs for 'OutOfMemoryError', 'Container killed by YARN', 'GC overhead limit exceeded'), on heap-used > 85% and GC time > 15% thresholds, and on non-zero disk spill for stages expected to fit in memory, so pressure is caught before the job fails.

recommendedPractices: **Diagnose the OOM signature first:** Determine whether it is Java heap space (heap/partition/skew), a container kill (overhead/python), or GC overhead (heap/cores/off-heap) before changing any config.
**Size overhead explicitly for PySpark:** Set spark.executor.memoryOverhead to ~15-20% of heap and cap spark.executor.pyspark.memory so python workers cannot silently blow the container.
**Bound per-partition size:** Target ~100-200MB per partition via spark.sql.shuffle.partitions/repartition so per-task memory stays constant as data grows.
**Prefer fewer cores per executor for memory-heavy work:** Reducing spark.executor.cores gives each task a larger heap share and cuts OOM without adding RAM.
**Never collect/toPandas large data:** Filter/aggregate first, use toLocalIterator() or write() for large outputs, and keep broadcasts small.
engineeringStandards: Enable -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError with a secured HeapDumpPath and GC logging (-XX:+PrintGCDetails) in production so every OOM leaves evidence.
Enable Adaptive Query Execution (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true) including skew join handling as a default for runtime partition and skew correction.
Document the memory arithmetic (reserved/user/unified split and container total) for every production executor template so overhead is never forgotten.
designRecommendations: Push filters and projections before shuffles to shrink the data that must fit in execution memory.
Broadcast small dimension tables to avoid shuffle-side memory pressure, and keep broadcast size well under a few hundred MB.
Enable off-heap (spark.memory.offHeap) only when GC is the proven bottleneck on large binary working sets, and always account for its size in the container total.
namingConventions: Name executor templates by their memory profile (e.g., mem-heavy-8g-3core, balanced-6g-4core) so the sizing intent is explicit in job configs.
Set descriptive spark.app.name and spark.job.description so OOM incidents in the History Server map clearly to the responsible pipeline and stage.
documentationStandards: Record the expected container total (heap + overhead + off-heap + python) in the runbook so on-call can verify the resource request matches the node capacity.
Document known skewed keys and the mitigation (salting, AQE skew handling) alongside the memory config for each job.
Capture a baseline of GC time, spill, and peak heap so regressions (rising GC/spill) are easy to detect after code or data changes.
testingStrategies: Run the job at 1.5-2x expected data volume in staging to confirm memory headroom before production data growth causes OOM.
Inject skew (a synthetic hot key) in tests to verify AQE skew handling and partition sizing prevent single-task OOM.
Assert broadcast sizes and shuffle partition counts in unit tests to catch accidental large broadcasts or under-partitioning that would cause OOM.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reflexively increasing spark.executor.memory for a 'Container killed by YARN' error.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Engineers conflate the container kill with a heap OOM and assume more heap always helps.
commonMistakes.impact: The container total grows but the overhead/python shortfall remains, so kills continue; the larger heap also lengthens GC pauses and wastes RAM.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Read the message — 'consider boosting spark.executor.memoryOverhead' — and raise memoryOverhead (and cap spark.executor.pyspark.memory) instead of the heap.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling collect() or toPandas() on a large DataFrame.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is the easy way to inspect or post-process results locally, and works fine on small data during development.
commonMistakes.impact: All partitions are pulled into the driver JVM at once, causing java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space and taking down the driver/application.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Aggregate/filter to a small result before collecting, use toLocalIterator() to stream partitions, or write() results to storage; raise spark.driver.memory only for legitimately bounded results.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running too many cores per executor for memory-heavy tasks.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Maximizing cores per executor seems to maximize parallelism and cluster utilization.
commonMistakes.impact: All concurrent tasks share one heap, so each gets a small memory share; heavy tasks OOM or thrash GC (GC overhead limit exceeded) as the JVM fills.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Reduce spark.executor.cores (e.g., 5 to 3) so each task gets a larger memory share, trading a little parallelism for stability.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring skew and tuning only average memory.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Sizing is done from average partition size, hiding that a few hot keys produce giant partitions.
commonMistakes.impact: One task's partition dwarfs the rest and OOMs regardless of average sizing, failing the whole stage after retries.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Detect skew in the Stages tab (one task far longer/larger), then salt the key, use AQE skew join handling, or increase partitions to split the hot data.

comparisonSection.feature: OOM failure signature and its correct fix
comparisonSection.optionB: Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits
comparisonSection.explanation: A heap-space OOM means a task's live objects exceeded the JVM heap; fixes are more heap, more partitions, avoiding huge collect/broadcast, or fixing skew. A container kill means the total physical footprint (heap + off-heap + overhead + python) exceeded the container limit; the fix is raising spark.executor.memoryOverhead and capping spark.executor.pyspark.memory, not the heap. Misreading one for the other wastes tuning effort.

The static manager hard-split the heap into fixed execution and storage fractions, so a shuffle could OOM while cache space sat empty. The unified manager (default) shares one region (spark.memory.fraction) where execution can evict storage down to the storageFraction floor, eliminating many avoidable OOMs and requiring far less manual tuning.

On-heap memory is managed by the JVM and subject to garbage collection, which causes pauses and GC-overhead failures on very large working sets. Off-heap stores serialized data in native memory outside GC, reducing pauses for large binary sets, but it must be explicitly sized and counts toward the container total, so enabling it without raising the container limit trades a heap OOM for a container kill.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does spark.executor.memory control, and is it the total memory an executor uses?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It sets the JVM on-heap size of each executor. It is not the total: the container also includes spark.executor.memoryOverhead (JVM internals, Netty, native), off-heap memory if enabled, and the PySpark python worker, so the true container footprint is heap + off-heap + overhead + python.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize that forgetting overhead is why containers get killed even when the heap looks adequate.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is spark.executor.memoryOverhead and what is its default?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It is non-heap memory reserved in the container for JVM overhead, Netty network buffers, and native/python usage. The default is max(384MB, 0.1 * spark.executor.memory).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tie it directly to the 'Container killed by YARN ... consider boosting spark.executor.memoryOverhead' message as the canonical fix.

intermediateQuestions.question: Walk through how spark.executor.memory is divided by the Unified Memory Manager.
intermediateQuestions.answer: Spark first reserves a fixed 300MB, leaving usable = executor memory - 300MB. Usable is split into user memory = (1 - spark.memory.fraction) * usable (default 0.4) and the unified region = spark.memory.fraction * usable (default 0.6). The unified region is elastically shared between execution and storage, with a soft floor for storage at spark.memory.storageFraction (default 0.5) that execution cannot evict below.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The key insight is the elastic execution/storage sharing with the storage floor, versus the old static split.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you tell apart a Java heap OOM, a container kill, and a GC overhead error, and how does the fix differ?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Java heap space OOM = task exceeded the JVM heap (fix: more heap, more partitions, avoid huge collect/broadcast, fix skew). Container killed = total physical footprint exceeded the container (fix: raise memoryOverhead, cap pyspark.memory). GC overhead limit exceeded = JVM spends >98% time in GC reclaiming <2% heap (fix: more heap, fewer cores per executor, off-heap). Each maps to a different knob.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This diagnostic triage is the single most important operational skill for this topic.

advancedQuestions.question: A PySpark job with a pandas UDF keeps getting containers killed even after doubling spark.executor.memory. Why, and what do you do?
advancedQuestions.answer: The pandas UDF runs in separate python worker processes whose RSS lives outside the JVM heap and draws from container headroom. Doubling the heap raises the container total but does not give python more room relative to the limit, and can worsen GC. The fix is to raise spark.executor.memoryOverhead and set spark.executor.pyspark.memory to bound python worker memory, and possibly reduce cores so fewer python workers run concurrently per executor.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Highlight that python memory is off-heap and often the hidden cause of PySpark container kills.

advancedQuestions.question: When and why would you reduce spark.executor.cores to solve an OOM?
advancedQuestions.answer: Each executor runs spark.executor.cores tasks concurrently, all sharing one heap, so execution memory is divided among them. For memory-heavy tasks, too many cores means each task's share is too small, causing heap OOM or GC thrashing. Reducing cores (e.g., 5 to 3) enlarges each task's memory share, trading some parallelism for stability, which is often cheaper than adding RAM.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Connect concurrency to per-task memory share; mention it also reduces the number of concurrent python workers in PySpark.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your nightly job intermittently fails with both 'Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits' on some runs and 'java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space' on others. It uses a pandas UDF and a wide groupBy on a skewed key. How do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Two signatures mean two root causes. The container kill points to overhead/python (the pandas UDF's python workers plus heap exceed the container). The heap-space OOM points to a giant partition from the skewed groupBy overflowing one task's execution memory. Fix each independently.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: For the container kill: raise spark.executor.memoryOverhead to ~15-20% of heap and set spark.executor.pyspark.memory to cap python workers. For the heap OOM: increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to shrink per-task data, enable AQE with skew join handling (or salt the hot key) to split the skewed partition, and reduce spark.executor.cores so each task gets more heap. Enable GC logging and -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError to confirm and capture evidence.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the executor memory configuration and OOM-resilience strategy for a PySpark pipeline processing 1TB of skewed event data with memory-heavy pandas UDFs on a cost-sensitive autoscaling cluster.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Choose moderate executors (e.g., 8g heap, 3 cores) rather than fat JVMs to bound GC and per-task memory. Compute the container total = 8g heap + ~1.5-2g overhead + spark.executor.pyspark.memory (2g) and ensure it fits node RAM. Target ~128MB partitions via spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, enable AQE with skew handling, broadcast small dimensions, and enable off-heap only if GC proves to be the bottleneck. Enable GC logs and heap dumps for diagnostics.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Fewer cores per executor stabilize memory but reduce parallelism; larger overhead and pyspark.memory reserve safe headroom but reduce heap available for execution; off-heap avoids GC but adds to the container total and must be sized carefully. Right-sizing beats over-provisioning for cost but requires profiling.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Keep per-partition working set constant as data grows by scaling partition count, and add executors (horizontal) rather than growing heaps. Enable the external shuffle service so OOM-induced executor loss recovers via stage retry without full recomputation, and set alerts on GC time, heap usage, and spill to catch pressure before failure.

How does enabling off-heap memory change the container total, and what must you also adjust?
Why can a bigger heap sometimes make performance worse?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Executor memory tuning sizes the JVM heap (reserved 300MB + user memory + unified execution/storage region), off-heap memory, and container overhead so tasks fit without a heap OOM or a container kill, and OOM debugging triages the failure signature to the right knob.
keyConcepts: Heap split: 300MB reserved, then user = (1 - memory.fraction) and unified = memory.fraction (0.6) of usable.
Unified region is elastic execution+storage with a storageFraction (0.5) floor.
Container total = heap + off-heap + memoryOverhead + python worker.
Three OOM signatures: Java heap space, Container killed by YARN, GC overhead limit exceeded.
Fewer cores per executor = larger per-task memory share.
formulas: Container total = heap + off-heap size + memoryOverhead + pyspark.memory
commands: --conf spark.executor.pyspark.memory=2g  # cap PySpark python worker memory
interviewPoints: spark.executor.memory is only the heap; the container is larger by overhead + off-heap + python.
'Container killed by YARN' is fixed with memoryOverhead/pyspark.memory, not more heap.
Java heap space OOM is fixed with more partitions, less collect/broadcast, or skew handling.
Since Spark 1.6 execution and storage share one unified region with a storage floor.
Reducing executor cores raises each task's memory share and cuts OOM/GC thrashing.
quickNotes: Target ~100-200MB per partition to keep per-task memory bounded.
Non-zero disk spill in the Stages tab = the stage is memory-starved.
GC time > ~10% of task time signals heap pressure (add heap, fewer cores, off-heap).
toLocalIterator()/write() replace collect()/toPandas() for large data.
On Kubernetes a container kill shows as OOMKilled / exit code 137.

keyTakeaways: An executor's heap is split by the Unified Memory Manager into a fixed 300MB reserved region, user memory ((1 - spark.memory.fraction)), and an elastic unified execution/storage region (spark.memory.fraction, default 0.6) with a storage floor at spark.memory.storageFraction (0.5).

The true container footprint is heap + off-heap (spark.memory.offHeap.size) + spark.executor.memoryOverhead (default max(384MB, 0.1*heap)) + the PySpark python worker, which is why containers get killed even when the heap looks fine.

The three OOM signatures map to different fixes: Java heap space (more partitions, less collect/broadcast, fix skew, more heap), Container killed by YARN (raise memoryOverhead, cap pyspark.memory), and GC overhead limit exceeded (more heap, fewer cores, off-heap).

Debug with the Executors tab (GC time, storage memory, failed tasks), the Stages tab (spill), GC logs (-XX:+PrintGCDetails), and heap dumps (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError); non-zero spill and high GC time are the early warnings before failure.

The cleanest OOM fixes are usually structural — bound per-partition size to ~100-200MB, reduce cores per executor, broadcast small tables, fix skew, and avoid materializing large data on one JVM — rather than reflexively raising spark.executor.memory.
